questions.prompt: Which line gives the three forms of the verb correctly (infinitive – past – past participle)?

options.text: grow – grew – growed
know – known – knew
say – sayed – said
keep – kept – kept

questions.explanation: "keep – kept – kept" is the correct line: this verb uses one single form for the past and for the past participle. "grow – grew – growed" invents a regular -ed ending where the participle is "grown"; "say – sayed – said" does the same in the past form, which is "said"; and "know – known – knew" has the last two columns the wrong way round, since the past is "knew" and the participle is "known".

questions.prompt: Mouna is talking about her future. Which sentence expresses a want or a desire?

options.text: I'd like to work in a laboratory one day.
My elder sister works in a laboratory.
I became interested in biology at ten.
I know two people who work in a laboratory.

questions.explanation: "I'd like to work in a laboratory one day." expresses a desire: I'd like is the short form of I would like, and it is followed by to + a base verb to name what you wish to do. "My elder sister works in a laboratory." describes what somebody else does now, "I became interested in biology at ten." narrates a past event, and "I know two people who work in a laboratory." states what Mouna knows, not what she wants.

questions.prompt: Sarra has had a hard year at school and often wants to give up. Her mother listens to her every evening and gives her the strength to carry on. Which word from the lesson names what her mother gives her?

options.text: security
trouble
support
a path

questions.explanation: "support" is right: support is the help that keeps somebody going when things are hard, and that is exactly what Sarra's mother gives her every evening. "trouble" names the difficulty itself, the hard year Sarra is living through, and not the help she receives against it. "security" is the feeling that nothing bad can reach you, whereas Sarra's year shows that plenty of hard things do reach her. And "a path" is the way you choose for your life, a direction rather than the strength to keep walking.

questions.prompt: Emna tells you: "I haven't chosen my future job yet." What does she mean?

options.text: She has chosen it, but she keeps her choice secret.
She has not chosen it, and the choice is still open.
She chose a job last year and then changed her mind about it.
She will never be able to choose a job for herself.

questions.explanation: "She has not chosen it, and the choice is still open." is right: haven't + past participle with yet means not up to now, and yet says that the choice is still expected. "She has chosen it, but she keeps her choice secret." turns the negative into an affirmative; "She chose a job last year and then changed her mind about it." invents a past event that Emna never mentions; and "She will never be able to choose a job for herself." reads yet as never, whereas yet leaves the door open.

questions.prompt: Khaled says: "I passed my driving test two months ago." Why can he not use the present perfect here?

options.text: Because passing a test is too short an event for that tense.
Because he names a moment that is over.
Because the present perfect has no negative form.
Because he is talking about himself and not about somebody else.

questions.explanation: "Because he names a moment that is over." is the reason: two months ago dates the event and closes it, and a present perfect never stands beside a named past moment. "Because passing a test is too short an event for that tense." invents a rule about length, when the present perfect accepts events of any length. "Because the present perfect has no negative form." is simply untrue, since I have not passed my test is a perfectly ordinary sentence. And "Because he is talking about himself and not about somebody else." confuses the person with the tense, when the subject decides nothing here.
